He was a passenger in a car that was rear-ended and hit multiple times, feeling two bumps that slung him forward and caused him to stretch out his right index finger. He states it has been hurting and swollen ever since, he cannot make a fist, sometimes the pain is unbearable, and even driving hurts. 

He previously saw an orthopedist at Point May Orthopedics, was sent to an occupational therapist, and had an MRI obtained on 4/24/2021. He reports being told he had a tear in his finger. He was previously advised against an injection because it could make the tear worse, and subsequently offered an injection after the MRI, leading him to seek a second opinion as he feels he is not getting proper medical care. He works as an x-ray tech and is right-handed. 

Prior Imaging & Diagnostics:
- X-rays (four views of the right hand today): No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits on the right hand, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no arthritis.
- MRI (4/24/2021): Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of the right FDS, and fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint were intact, as was the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons deemed intact.

Past Medical History & Medications:
- Diabetes: None
- Rheumatoid Arthritis: None
- Chronic Medications: Takes a blood pressure pill.
- Allergies/Adverse Reactions: Methylprednisolone (causes itching); dexamethasone (causes his heart to race).

Physical Exam:
- General: Very pleasant, cooperative, healthy male, no distress.
- Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulses.
- Right Hand / Index Finger: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases, slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in a 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Pushing on the PIP is uncomfortable; other areas feel a little numb. Bending the tip and the finger elicits pain described as feeling like it is tearing. Bending at the MCP joint causes pain, attributed to stretching due to prolonged immobility. Extensor tendons, collateral ligaments, and the FDP tendon (going to the tip) are intact.

Assessment:
Post-traumatic rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger, with a partial-thickness tear of one half of the FDS (flexor digitorum superficialis) tendon. Substantial scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS tendon are blocking excursion of the other tendons.

Plan / Procedure:
1. Steroid injection attempted using 1 cc of Celestone (betamethasone, water-soluble, low toxicity) with 0.5 cc of lidocaine to decrease pain and inflammation and encourage finger movement. 
2. Injection Course: During the first attempt, the patient had a dramatic and violent painful reaction to the introduction of the needle with hand contortions and dangerous withdrawal with concerns for secondary needle stick; the needle was withdrawn. After counseling, a second attempt was made using the same technique with 1 cc of Celestone and 0.5 cc of lidocaine. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned up and a band-aid applied. The patient was reassured that no harm was done to his finger.
3. Post-procedure care: Recommended icing the finger this evening and taking ibuprofen. Expected to take 3 to 5 days to start feeling better, and over the next couple of weeks to improve further. 
4. Physical Therapy: Outpatient occupational therapy once a week for six weeks to work toward full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. 
5. Activity: Safe to drive, though it may feel a little weird. Must actively move the finger to address the stiffness.

The patient is a female presenting with right ankle pain after slipping and falling on ice yesterday while taking out the trash. She reports hearing a pop when she fell. Initially, she was completely unable to walk on the ankle, and a visiting friend helped her inside. Today, she is able to put a little bit more weight on it, though she is still limping. She has treated the injury by icing it last night, keeping it elevated, and taking ibuprofen last night and this morning before the visit. Without ibuprofen, her pain level is a 6 out of 10. With ibuprofen, her pain level decreases to a 1 out of 10 (she currently rates her pain at a 4 out of 10). She denies any numbness or tingling in the right foot. She has a history of playing soccer in college and intramural soccer currently, but has not been able to play since the injury. She has a history of injuries to her other ankle, but has never injured this right ankle before.

Physical Exam:
Vitals look good and normal.
Focused exam of the right ankle:
- Ecchymosis/bruising observed over the lateral malleolus.
- Edema/swelling present in that area.
- Positive for tenderness to palpation of the anterolateral soft tissue.
- No laxity appreciated on anterior drawer and inversion stress.
- No bony tenderness on palpation to the foot or ankle area.
Neurovascular exam of the right foot:
- Brisk capillary refill of less than 3 seconds.
- Strong dorsalis pedis pulse.
- Sensation intact to light touch.
Findings are consistent with the left side.

Diagnostic Results:
X-ray of the right ankle showed no fracture.

Assessment and Plan:
- Problem: Right ankle pain.
- Symptoms are consistent with a right ankle sprain of the lateral ligament complex, more specifically the anterior talofibular ligament on the outside of the ankle which was stretched during the fall.
- Treatment: 
  - Keep the leg elevated when seated.
  - Continue to ice.
  - Patient will be given an air cast to help stabilize the ankle.
  - Prescribed crutches to stay off the leg for now, then start walking on it as tolerated in a couple of days.
  - Continue to take NSAIDs or ibuprofen as needed for pain and to help reduce inflammation and swelling.
  - Symptoms should significantly improve over a few weeks.
  - Follow-up appointment scheduled in 14 days (two weeks) to see how she is doing.

Respiratory Rate: 18
Temperature: 97.1 F

Pulse: 60 beats per minute

Physical Exam:
General: Vitals look great.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmur, rub, or gallop appreciated.
Respiratory: Stridor appreciated; no wheezes or rales.
Abdominal: No rebound tenderness, no guarding.

Patient: Karen Nelson, 3-year-old female
Chief Complaint: New right eye twitch
History of Present Illness: The patient is accompanied by her father, who reports noticing a right eye twitch a couple of weeks ago and was advised by her pediatrician to seek evaluation. Karen states she feels her face sometimes when it happens. She reports no pain, but notes that her father looks nervous when it occurs. Karen reports feeling an urge to move her face, and then after it moves, she feels better. The father reports seeing the twitch several times an hour on some days, while on other days it is not seen until late afternoon, but they have definitely noticed it every day for the last several weeks. When the twitch happens, she just continues playing or doing whatever she was doing. The father reports she has been feeling fine overall, eating well, playing with friends, and going about her normal activities. The twitch involves the whole side of her face moving when it happens, lasting several seconds before finally stopping, followed by frequent blinking. The father brought a video of the twitch to show the physician.
Review of Systems: 
- Past medical history: None significant. No history of seizures.
- Family history: No history of seizures or Tourette's syndrome.
- Associated symptoms: Negative for fever, chills, coughing, and headache.
- Sleep: No problems with sleep.
Physical Examination:
- General: Awake, alert, and oriented times three. Speech is clear and fluent.
- Gait: Steady; heel-toe walking is normal.
- Cranial Nerves: Intact without focal neurologic findings. Followed finger with eyes.
- Motor: No pronator drift.
- Sensory: Sensation is intact to touch throughout.
- Reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at the biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles.
Assessment and Plan:
- Assessment: Transient tics. Eye tics are very common in children (as many as 1 in five children during school years) and can include brief, sudden, and involuntary motor movements such as shoulder shrugging, facial grimacing, sniffling, excessive throat clearing, and uncontrolled vocalization. Typically occur around 5 to 10 years of age, though Karen is 3. Most tics go away on their own and disappear within a year (transient tics). The cause is not fully understood. Symptoms may wax and wane over time and may be more noticeable towards the end of the day when tired or when stressed. 
- Plan: The best approach is to ignore the tics so as not to draw attention to them, which can make the child conscious and make the tic worse. Seizure is not suspected because the movement affects the same part of the body every time, and the patient reports an urge followed by relief. No medication (pills or creams) or treatment is recommended at this time because she is doing well overall and the tic has not impacted her school or activities. If it worsens, treatment can be considered in the future.

The patient has ten siblings and has been helping the brother cover extra work because they have been getting really busy.

Social History: Patient denies any history of seasonal allergies. Patient does not smoke and does not live with anyone who smokes.

Physical Exam:
Vitals: Respiratory rate is 20, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Heart: Regular rate and regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Fine rales present. No wheezes.
Musculoskeletal: No clubbing of the fingers.

Diagnostic Results:
Chest X-ray reviewed: showed ground-glass opacities.

Assessment and Plan:
- Problem: Recurrent lung infections, consistent with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, also known as farmer's lung, caused by inhaling bacteria and/or mold found in hay leading to an allergic reaction in the lungs.
- Prescribed a course of an oral steroid to decrease lung inflammation for current symptoms.
- Ordering a CT scan of the lungs to help confirm the diagnosis.
- Ordering a pulmonary function test to assess the severity of respiratory impairment.
- Recommendation to eliminate exposure to hay to prevent further lung damage, or if unable, to wear a respirator when moving hay around.

CHIEF COMPLAINT: Foot pain.

The patient's body twisted around the other player, resulting in pain in the foot. No prior injuries to this foot. The patient was unable to continue playing and had to stop right away, being helped off the field. Since the injury, the patient has been keeping it elevated, icing it, the trainer wrapped it yesterday, and taking ibuprofen. Pain level without ibuprofen is reported as a 3, and with ibuprofen is reported as a 7 to 8. Patient denies any numbness, tingling, or strange sensations in the left foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: Vitals reviewed: Blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 58, respiratory rate 14, afebrile, O2 saturation 99% on room air. Heart exam shows regular rate and rhythm, no clicks, rubs, or murmurs, no ectopic beats. Lung exam shows lungs clear and equal bilaterally.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Left foot exam: Bruising observed on the bottom and top of the foot. Associated swelling present. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive for the piano key test. 
Neurovascular exam of the left foot: Brisk capillary refill of less than 3 seconds, dorsalis pedis pulse intact and strong, motor and sensation intact to light touch.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING REVIEW: Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3 millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
- Right foot pain due to a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to one of the second metatarsal bones at the top of the foot where the metatarsals meet the cuboids).
- Ordering an MRI to assess for injury to the ligaments at the top of the foot.
- Based on exam and X-ray, surgery is most likely needed to place bones back in their proper position and hold them there using plates and screws to allow bones and ligaments to heal properly. This is a day surgery and the patient will go home the same day.
- Follow up in the clinic. Patient will be in a cast, will need to use crutches, and will not be able to use the left foot for about 6 to 8 weeks. After 6 to 8 weeks, the patient will gradually start walking on the foot based on tolerance.
- Surgery is recommended to prevent significant complications such as poor bone and ligament healing leading to a loss of the foot arch and becoming flat-footed, as well as a high likelihood of developing arthritis.
- Patient will be out for the rest of the season.
- Nurse will come in to start paperwork, and the patient will follow up on Monday morning.

REASON FOR VISIT: Nonhealing foot ulcer on the right foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: 
The patient is a male with diabetes and diabetic neuropathy who presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer on his right foot. He has been wearing a boot for about six weeks. He first noticed it after wearing a pair of shoes that were a little bit too tight, feeling burning and stinging, and finding a blister on the pad of the bottom of his foot around his heel. He had been walking on the front part of his foot. Recently, he noticed a foul smell, and his wife and dog also noticed the smell. They looked and saw that the blister had become unroofed with the top part of the skin undone, revealing thick, soft mushy skin underneath with a bad smell and yellow drainage. His wife called his primary care doctor, who started him on a 10-day course of antibiotics about 6 to 7 days ago. 

He never had nausea or vomiting. His wife checked his temperature, and it was 99.7. At one point, he had chills and had to put on an extra blanket in bed. When he started the antibiotics, it started to feel pretty good, but he has now noticed that it has turned black around the outside of the wound. He is getting cramping in his calf muscle, a red streak coming up the front part of his ankle along the inside portion of his calf muscle, and it is super hot. 

Initially, the wound was stinging, but at this point, it is throbbing like a fire poker is in the bottom of his foot. The inside of his calf muscle is really hard, and every time he pushes it, he feels it all the way up to his knee behind his kneecap. He has also been coughing a lot for the last two days and has had a difficult time catching his breath when walking around the house. 

Regarding his diabetes, his A1c is 6.7 and has been for about two years. He checks his blood sugar 2 to 3 times a day, or more if he feels weird, and rarely goes over 200. However, his sugars have been trending in the 300s to 400s over the last two weeks, with one spike at 500 to 600. 

Regarding the cause, he hikes with his wife and recently hiked to Charlie's Bunion about a week before this. He gets new diabetic shoes and inserts every year and changes inserts every 3 or 4 months. He got a new pair of shoes and went hiking about the third or fourth day, which he thinks might have caused it as he went too far.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
- Vital Signs: Slight fever noted; vitals themselves look good.
- Foot Exam: Necrotic wound on the heel, approximately 2 x 2 centimeters. Sloughing of the tissue is present, along with cellulitis and erythema around the area. Foul odor is present. No bony exposure is appreciated. Patient does not feel pressure when the actual affected area of the wound is pressed.
- Vascular Exam: Bilateral palpable femoral and popliteal pulses are present. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are not palpable, but are present via Doppler.

DIAGNOSTIC RESULTS:
- Right foot X-ray done today shows no evidence of osteomyelitis (no infection of the bone).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
- Nonhealing diabetic foot ulcer.
- Order a test to check blood supply for the wound.
- Perform a debridement today in the office.
- Perform a wound culture.
- Continue the current course of antibiotics prescribed by the primary care doctor (day 6 or 7 of a 10 to 12 day course), and determine if additional or changed antibiotic therapy is needed based on the culture results, addressing the redness moving up the leg and swelling/pain in the calf.
- Follow up in 7 days.
- Follow up with endocrinologist for diabetes management to keep hemoglobin A1c below 7 and closely monitor blood sugars given the antibiotic therapy and potential other medications.

Patient is a person with a history of headaches since they were a teenager, initially associated with menses and stress. Recently, the headaches have increased in frequency and severity. Headaches are worsened by exercise, specifically jogging, which makes them come on a lot worse. Associated symptoms include ringing in the ears for a few months and intermittent blurred vision on the side of their vision. Denies numbness or tingling in hands, feet, or face. Uses Asics shoes for running.

Prior medical history includes an MRI of the brain from a few years ago. 

Physical exam:
Vitals: Reviewed vitals collected by the assistant, including blood pressure, and everything looks good.
Heart exam: Normal sinus rhythm with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Funduscopic exam: Shows papilledema (swelling behind the eye).
Neurological exam: Cranial nerves 1 through 12 are intact, including a normal cranial reflex.
Musculoskeletal exam: Gait is normal when walking across the room and turning around.

Assessment:
Symptoms are concerning for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (increased pressure in the head/brain without a known cause), presenting with headaches worsening with activity, ringing in the ears, and changes in vision. Concern exists that if pressure continues to increase, it can lead to permanent changes in vision.

Plan:
1. Order a recent MRI of the brain (team in the front office will work on insurance preapproval and call to schedule once complete) to check for any other contributing conditions.
2. Perform a spinal tap after MRI results to evaluate brain pressure and help reduce pressure.
3. Refer to a neuro-ophthalmologist for a complete eye exam.
4. Discussed that if the diagnosis is confirmed, treatment does not necessarily mean surgery; a number of medications can be used to decrease brain pressure and help reduce headaches during exercise. Exercise and weight loss are also important parts of the treatment.

Patient has two inhalers but primarily uses her blue rescue inhaler, identified as albuterol (ventolin); she states the other inhaler does not work when she tries to use it. Routinely exposed to secondhand smoke when she occasionally goes to bars with friends, which irritates her, so she tries not to go often.

He reports numbness and tingling, especially to his right leg going down to his foot. He denies loss of sensation in the genital or rectal area, denies weakness, and denies loss of control of his bladder or bowels. He tries to be as active as he can, but it is difficult, and he has gained weight over the past years. He has been trying to get into golf, but the back pain has set him back.

FAMILY HISTORY: No family members with spine conditions.

SOCIAL HISTORY: Quit smoking about 20 years ago.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Vitals: Reviewed and overall look pretty good.
Musculoskeletal / Back: No overlying erythema or ecchymosis. Midline tenderness at L4-L5 disc space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Pain with lumbar flexion. Supine straight leg test is positive.
Neurological: Decreased sensation to light touch at the right lateral thigh at L4 dermatome. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are symmetrical and good.

REVIEW OF DIAGNOSTIC STUDIES: MRI reviewed, showing disc herniation with nerve impingement.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Chronic lumbar back pain. Symptoms, exam, and MRI results are consistent with an L4-L5 herniated disc with radiculopathy, where a disc between the spinal vertebrae is bulging out and pinching on nerves, causing tingling in the leg. 

Recommended spinal injection with a strong anti-inflammatory medication called a corticosteroid, to be injected into the lumbar spine under fluoroscopy (X-ray guidance) to localize the exact area of pain and help the inflammation causing the pain. Discussed that intervals can vary by patient response, and they are usually not done more than four times a year. The procedure is quick and common, with the patient expected to be out of the office within an hour. The first injection will be initiated today or scheduled.

Patient is a 54-year-old male presenting for evaluation of facial pain. He reports a stabbing, shooting, excruciating pain in his right face and cheekbone area that sometimes gets super hot. The pain has been present for about two to three months, coming on slowly. Episodes last anywhere from a few minutes to about an hour, generally a few minutes, and rate a 10 in severity when they occur. The pain is triggered by certain temperatures, super cold, and outside wind. He has tried ibuprofen, motrins, and tiger balm, which have not helped. He was referred by his family doctor to see a neurosurgeon. He denies sensory loss such as numbness or tingling initially noticed, denies symptoms anywhere else on his face or the left side of his face, and denies facial weakness when smiling or doing other things. His vision is unchanged. He denies a history of multiple sclerosis or brain tumors. He gets occasional headaches that resolve with Tylenol, but no history of migraines.

Physical examination:
Cranial nerve and motor exam shows smile is equal on both sides, eyes show no weakness, and vision is unchanged. Follows finger in both directions. Teeth show nice and symmetric appearance. Hearing is intact bilaterally to finger rub. Cotton test along the side of the face shows it feels a little bit numb on the right side, not so much on the left side. Needle test shows the right side feels a little bit dull, while the left side feels sharp.

Imaging:
MRI review shows a small blood vessel that is abutting and perhaps even pinching the trigeminal nerve.

Assessment:
Trigeminal neuralgia, caused by nerve compression from a blood vessel against the trigeminal nerve resulting in shooting electrical pain in the face.

Plan:
1. Start first-line medical treatment with Tegretol to reduce nerve excitability. 
2. Discuss potential side effects of Tegretol, including memory loss, tingling, imbalance, and dermatologic skin reactions.
3. Perform genetic testing prior to starting Tegretol due to considerations for certain ancestry (e.g., eustachian descent).
4. Send prescription for Tegretol to the patient's pharmacy.
5. Follow up in one month to check the effectiveness of the medication, and discuss surgical options to decompress the nerve if medications are insufficient.

Patient Name: Jordan Roberts
DOB: 3/2/1972
Age: 49 years old

Reason for Visit: New patient visit for hypertension and palpitations. Thyroid profile from March 1st, 2021 to be copied forward.

History of Present Illness:
Patient presents for evaluation of hypertension and palpitations. He was recently in the emergency room in March with high blood pressure and palpitations. He attributes this episode to having a few cups of coffee and no breakfast that day, believing it was likely a panic attack. He reports no recurrence of palpitations since. 
Patient has had issues with high blood pressure since he was young, and notes a strong family history of high blood pressure. About a month ago, his new primary care doctor started him on a combination medication, Benicar HCT 40-25 (hydrochlorothiazide/olmesartan). He is also taking amlodipine 10 milligrams daily. He checks his blood pressure every morning upon waking; recent readings have been running between 146 and 155. 
Regarding lifestyle, he is trying to back off on salt intake and feels he is doing well not eating too much salt. He tries to walk on the treadmill when he can. 
Discussed resistant hypertension, secondary causes (such as parathyroid levels or overproduction of aldosterone by adrenal glands/hyperaldosteronism), and potential need for further evaluation if blood pressure remains uncontrolled.

Physical Examination:
General: Exam performed using general physical exam template.
Heart and Lungs: Heart and lungs sound good.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no pain to palpation anywhere.
Extremities: Ankles and feet checked for swelling; no edema noted, all looks good.

Assessment and Plan:
- Resistant hypertension, uncontrolled despite being on three medications at maximum doses.
- Added spironolactone to the regimen to help drop aldosterone levels and blood pressure.
- Discussed risks associated with hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone:
  - Electrolyte balance and dehydration: Patient must hydrate to avoid dizziness when standing up.
  - Spironolactone can raise potassium; baseline potassium one week ago was 4.0, providing a safe starting window. Potassium has not been redone in the last week.
  - Combination of spironolactone and hydrochlorothiazide can lower sodium levels (does not mean patient needs to eat more salt).
  - Potential side effects including dizziness and rare gynecomastia (chest tenderness, swollen or enlarged breasts in 1 in 100 men; patient instructed to stop medication and notify provider if this occurs).
- Ordered blood tests (metabolic panel to check potassium and sodium/electrolytes) and scheduled a follow-up appointment in two weeks to check blood pressure and electrolytes.
- Next medication considered would be carvedilol, though provider tries to avoid giving it due to the potential for erectile dysfunction (which was discussed with the patient).
- If the new medication is ineffective, the next step will be referral to the resistant hypertension clinic to look into secondary causes of hypertension and discuss procedure-based technologies such as renal denervation.
- Provided education on the DASH eating plan, heart.org website, reducing sodium intake to under 2000 mg/day (ideal 1500 mg/day), increasing potassium, and performing routine treadmill exercise for 30 minutes most days to potentially lower blood pressure by 7 to 10 points. Reviewed the importance of blood pressure control in preventing heart enlargement, heart failure, kidney failure, and stroke.

The patient is a 39-year-old female with a history of quadriplegia due to a prior spinal cord injury, presenting for follow-up after an admission to District Regional Hospital from 06/29/2021 to 07/02/2021. She believes her hospitalization symptoms, including high blood pressure, headache, and vomiting, were caused by severe constipation rather than a UTI. She also has lactulose in a bottle for rescue use, noting it takes about two days to work and is brutal, but effective. She notes that the period leading up to her hospitalization was extremely hot and humid, and she stays in more when it is hot.

She feels she is young and healthy enough to beat the virus despite her limited respiratory function, takes vitamin C and multivitamins, is closely monitored, and does not feel she needs the vaccine. General appearance: Feels back to normal, no acute distress.

Acute to Chronic Constipation: The patient believes her hospitalization was due to autonomic dysreflexia secondary to severe constipation. Plan: Patient will return in two to three weeks for complete blood work, including a CBC with white blood cells to ensure counts are trending downward, and a full lipid panel for cholesterol.

Quadriplegia: Stable history, managed with a supra-pubic catheter.

Plan: Discussed vaccine safety and efficacy. Provider recommended vaccination, noting the patient is at high risk due to quadriplegia and that supplements will not prevent COVID-19. The patient is open-minded and will think about it.

History of Present Illness:
Ashley is a 14-year-old previously healthy female who presented for evaluation of an abnormal renal ultrasound showing a small, atrophic right kidney. The history began when Ashley came home sick out of nowhere, rubbing her stomach and complaining of right-sided pain so severe she was bent over. They initially thought it was appendicitis and took her to her doctor, who treated her for a stomach virus, gave her fluids, and sent her home. The next day she was twice as bad. 

The mother took her back for more testing, including an ultrasound, which showed one kidney was bigger. They were told to follow up with her primary care physician the next day, but he was heading out on vacation and only saw her for a brief 10 minutes. Because she was still throwing up and in a lot of pain, the mother took work off to help her and took her to Jacksonville, where providers stated they did not think one of her kidneys was working at all, calling it atrophic and much smaller than the other. They also found cysts on her kidney and ovaries and potentially other places, swollen lymph nodes, and an infection. 

When they followed up with her primary doctor a day or two later, he was still out of town with no coverage. They then went to Atlanta, staying for about four days, where she was seen and treated. Since then, her vomiting has resolved, but she still complains of a lot of stomach pain and burning, especially when she eats. She also reports burning when she pees, particularly when she drinks certain beverages like soda, so she now only drinks water or Gatorade. Sometimes she reports it is hard to start urinating. - History of severe infection(s) at age 4, hospitalized 3 or 4 times for about three days at a time. Received fluids and antibiotics and sent home, with symptoms returning a week or two later over the course of a couple of months before stopping. Doctor at the time suspected she has had kidney problems since then.
- Seen by GI and a geneticist; panel showed no clinically significant mutations.

Medications:
- Pepcid 40 mg daily
- Claritin for allergies

Family History:
- Renal disease runs in the maternal family (grandfather, aunt, and cousins have kidney issues).
- Grandfather had obstructive neuropathy/posterior urethral valves, developed chronic kidney disease, was dialysis-dependent, had a renal transplant which subsequently failed, and died at age 47 of a massive heart attack (noted to have been utilizing dialysis).
